h1:
Tai Lue Food in Chiang Kham
Local Dishes & Community Spots
intro: Chiang Kham is a small district in eastern Phayao, but it's home to the Tai Lue people who migrated here from Sipsong Panna (Xishuangbanna) centuries ago. The food has a flavor and a look all its own — different from the usual northern Thai cooking, with fermented and sun-dried specialties and chili dips you'd be hard pressed to find anywhere else. We've eaten our way through the Tai Lue villages here and picked out what's worth trying and which spots are still going.
chips: 🌶️ Chili dips you won't find elsewhere

blocks.html: The Tai Lue of Chiang Kham settled around Ban That Sop Waen, Ban Yuan and Ban Mang, clustered near old temples like Wat Phra That Sop Waen and Wat Saen Mueang Ma. The community's own slogan even spells out its food in plain terms — ‘kalamae from Ban That Sop Waen, khanom pat from Ban Yuan, come try khao kaep from Ban Mang’ — which tells you food is the heart of the place. Come to Chiang Kham and eat nothing but khao soi nam ngiao, and you've missed a lot of the real thing.

Tai Lue cooking is built on preserving food — fermenting, pickling, drying, and chili dips pounded to eat with steamed vegetables. It isn't as fierce as Isan food, but it has a deep savory pull from the ferments and the local herbs. These are the dishes people in Chiang Kham actually eat day to day.

items.name: Jin som (jin sam)
items.blurb: Pork or beef fermented with cooked rice until it turns naturally sour — like naem, but the Tai Lue version. Eat it raw with ginger and fresh chili, or fry, grill, or stir-fry it with egg. It's the house ferment nearly every kitchen in Chiang Kham keeps on hand.

items.name: Nam prik nam pu
items.blurb: A chili dip made from rice-paddy crab simmered down to a thick, dark paste, pounded with chilies and herbs. The smell is strong but the flavor is deeply savory. People in Chiang Kham eat it with steamed veg and sticky rice — for the full Tai Lue combo, get it alongside khao kaep crackers to dip.
items.meta: Local chili dip · eaten with steamed veg

items.name: Khao kaep (Ban Mang)
items.blurb: Thin sheets of sticky-rice batter scattered with sesame and dried in the sun, then grilled or toasted until they puff up crisp. Eat them as a snack or use them to scoop chili dip. Ban Mang is so well known for these that they've become Chiang Kham's signature thing to take home.

items.name: Gaeng pak kat som (sour mustard-green curry)
items.blurb: A clear curry with sour pickled mustard greens and pork or pork rib — a mild, well-rounded sourness. It's a Tai Lue home staple that goes down easy, and just the thing on a day you want something hot to slurp.

items.name: Northern larb (larb khua)
items.blurb: Northern-style larb with fragrant roasted larb spices, no toasted rice powder like the Isan version. Some places do a bitter larb with phlia (cattle bile) for that savory-bitter edge locals like. Eat it with fresh veg and hot sticky rice.

items.name: Sa (sa pak / sa jin)
items.blurb: A northern-style herb salad — vegetables or cooked meat tossed with sa seasoning and lime juice for a fresh, sour kick. It's a good opener for a meal, light on the stomach and a nice cut against anything fried.

items.name: Jin sam prik
items.blurb: Fermented meat tossed with chili Tai Lue style — sour and spicy on the tip of the tongue, the kind of thing you can't stop eating with sticky rice. It's hard to find outside Chiang Kham.

items.name: Grilled stuffed fish (tilapia/freshwater fish)
items.blurb: Freshwater fish stuffed with lemongrass and herb leaves, wrapped and grilled until fragrant — tender, not fishy. It's a dish traditional Tai Lue houses like to make for guests. Eat it with chili dip and steamed veg.

items.name: Khanom pat (Ban Yuan)
items.blurb: A thick, sticky sweet made from rice flour stirred with sugar and coconut milk, simmered long until it turns deep brown. It's the original recipe behind Chiang Kham's kalamae, made for merit-making and for guests during Songkran and the northern new year.

items.name: Old-style kalamae (Ban That Sop Waen)
items.blurb: A chewy stirred sweet, the Tai Lue recipe that grew out of khanom pat, fragrant with coconut milk and cane sugar. It's a Chiang Kham souvenir you can pick up at the morning market and at community shops.

blocks.title: Local tip
blocks.html: Ferments and dried foods like jin som and khao kaep are sold at Chiang Kham's morning market before the sky even lightens. If you want them freshly made and the full range, get there before 8am and you'll have more to choose from. Kalamae and khanom pat tend to sell out fast during festivals.

blocks.text: Community spots that are still open

blocks.html: Chiang Kham doesn't have flashy big-sign Tai Lue restaurants. Most are humble home kitchens run by people in the community who've been cooking this way for years. These are the spots locals mention and that are still open right now — friendly prices, mostly around 70–130 baht a plate.

items.name: Moyo Lue (Tai Lue restaurant)
items.blurb: A spot in the Chiang Kham town area, set on a river bend in a raised wooden house. The name means ‘our Lue kin.’ The standouts are Chiang Kham-style cooked pork larb, cooked sa, tom saeb, a mixed fried platter, and fried naem ribs. Around 70–130 baht a plate.

items.name: Larb Lung Rop
items.blurb: An old larb shop open for more than 40 years, just across from Wat Phra Nang Din, serving both northern and Isan food. It's the place people in Chiang Kham think of when they want larb made the old-fashioned way.

items.name: Heuan Tai Lue Mae Saeng Da
items.blurb: A traditional Tai Lue house in the Ban Yuan community, where the owner — in her nineties — still keeps the old home and cooks proper Tai Lue food: jungle curry, grilled stuffed fish, and homemade sweets. A real way to experience Tai Lue life. Arrange it through the community in advance.

items.name: Chiang Kham morning market
items.blurb: The real treasure trove of local food, open at first light, with jin som, khao kaep, nam pu chili dip, khanom pat, kalamae, and all the local vegetables. You can graze and pick up souvenirs in one place.

blocks.text: A full day of Tai Lue eating

blocks.html: If you've got a day in Chiang Kham, here's an eating plan that takes you through Tai Lue flavors from morning to evening, with a temple and a weaving village worked in so you get both the food and the sights.

blocks.label: Morning
blocks.title: Morning market + ferments and dried foods

items.activity: Walk the Chiang Kham morning market and try grilled khao kaep with nam pu chili dip
items.note: Pick up jin som and kalamae to take home as souvenirs

items.activity: Stop by Wat Phra That Sop Waen to see the old chedi and the Tai Lue history hall
items.note: It's in the Ban That Sop Waen community — you can walk on to a weaving house

blocks.label: Midday
blocks.title: A proper Tai Lue main meal

items.activity: Have lunch at Moyo Lue — order cooked pork larb, cooked sa, and the mixed fried platter
items.note: It's down a lane in the town area, with parking on site

items.activity: Drop in at Wat Saen Mueang Ma for the Tai Lue architecture and murals
items.note: Close to town and an easy walk around

items.activity: Head to Ban Yuan to see the weaving and a traditional Tai Lue house
items.note: To eat authentic Tai Lue food at Heuan Mae Saeng Da, arrange it with the community ahead of time

items.activity: Finish with warm khanom pat and kalamae from the community
items.note: Buy some to take home — it keeps for several days

items: Bring cash — community spots and the morning market mostly take cash or PromptPay transfer, not cards.
Ferments have a strong flavor — jin som and nam pu chili dip are pungent and sour. If you've never had them, start with a little at a time.
Arrange ahead if you want to eat at a Tai Lue house — traditional houses take groups, so coordinate through the community center or a Chiang Kham tourism page first.
Buy souvenirs in the morning — khao kaep, kalamae and khanom pat are made fresh and sell out fast, especially during festivals.

faq.q: How is Tai Lue food in Chiang Kham different from regular northern Thai food?
faq.a: The Tai Lue have roots in Sipsong Panna (Xishuangbanna), so their food leans more on ferments, dried foods and local chili dips — things like jin som, khao kaep, nam pu chili dip and sour mustard-green curry. It isn't as fierce as Isan food, but it has a deep savory pull from the ferments and local herbs.

faq.q: Where can I eat authentic Tai Lue food in Chiang Kham?
faq.a: Moyo Lue in town serves Chiang Kham-style larb and sa, and Larb Lung Rop near Wat Phra Nang Din is a long-running old shop. For the real experience, head to Heuan Tai Lue Mae Saeng Da at Ban Yuan (arrange it ahead of time) and the Chiang Kham morning market, which has the full spread of local food.

faq.q: What souvenirs can I bring back from Chiang Kham?
faq.a: The standouts are old-style kalamae from Ban That Sop Waen, khanom pat from Ban Yuan, and khao kaep from Ban Mang. They all keep for several days and you'll find them at the morning market and community shops — along with jin som for anyone who likes ferments.

faq.q: What time does the Chiang Kham morning market open?
faq.a: It opens before the sky lightens and runs into mid-morning. If you want the full range of ferments, dried foods and freshly made sweets, go before 8am, since a lot of it is made fresh and sells out fast.

faq.q: How do you eat nam pu chili dip?
faq.a: Nam pu chili dip is made from rice-paddy crab simmered down thick — pungent but deeply savory. People in Chiang Kham eat it with steamed veg and sticky rice, or dip grilled khao kaep crackers in it for the full Tai Lue flavor. If you've never had it, start with a little, because the taste is bold and distinctive.
